utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nakic. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal. I am going to ask you, for the record, to begin by stating your full name and surname, your place and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: My name is Drago Nakic, I was born on the 17th of July, 1949 in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I am also going to ask you to bear in mind that we are speaking the same language so please make a pause between question and answer to facilitate the work of our interpreters. Mr. Nakic, are you married?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are a Croat by ethnicity of the Roman Catholic faith; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you have citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you additionally have citizenship of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The fact that you have citizenships, is it in keeping with both the republics?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you give your educational background?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of economics. I graduated in 1974 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And where do you work now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I work at the Vitezit Factory and it is one of the SPS Vitezit Cromen and it produces explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That part was previously known as what? What was its name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: The factory which was established in 1950 was entitled Slobodan Princip Seljo. However, as time went by, with the system of the organisations of associated labour, three compounds developed. The first was to produce military materiel, the second factory produced explosives for civilian purposes, civil engineering, and the third section was the production of plastics based on PVC and polyethylene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before these unfortunate times, that is to say, before the war in Bosnia, you were in the Vitezit factory producing explosives for civil engineering.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, explosives for civilian purposes in the field of mining, civil engineering, the building of tunnels and so on and so forth, civil engineering as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All these three factories were they in the same -- they were in the same location, were they not? And the popular term they were referred to was the SPS, is that right, by the locals? They referred to it as the SPS.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Because we all emanated from this first matrix factory, and the matrix factory had certain common functions in energetics, safety maintenance and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nakic, in the course of 1992 when the JNA had started its aggression in Bosnia, and when tensions grew, national tensions between all the nationalities, in the factory, at least the part of the factory that you were in and the people that you worked with and communicated with and met, did you notice any kind of change in their conduct in the relationship between Muslims and Croats, in particular?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is no doubt, and would you confirm this although the Court has already heard testimony on that account, just give us a yes or no answer, we have heard this many times, is it correct that the ethnic composition of the workers in the factory reflected the ethnic composition of the population, in general, in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. We took a great deal of care and attention to see that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, was there a reduction in the production capacities of the factory, that is to say, were production outputs lower?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I'd like to explain this by stating a fact, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Because relationships were severed with the former Yugoslavia, the factory lost its basic source of export because the part of the military factories were organised in that way that most of the finished products were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the raw materials were in Yugoslavia. And when these ties were severed, this meant that we had lost 70 per cent of our raw materials. We were no longer able to furnish the raw materials we needed. And because of Europe's relationship towards what was happening in the former Yugoslavia, there was no possibility of purchasing these raw materials in a European country and therefore, quite logically, it emanated from this that there was a drop-off in production levels. And people were sent to -- people were made to "stand by," as we called it. And they came from all the ethnic groups. They were put on standby.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When the multiparty system began to be set up and when the multiparty system was established, for the first time we had more than one party, political party, in our society. Did the management of the factory take any position vis-a-vis politics?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did the management of the factory in any way help the development and work of the parties at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The management of all three companies, was the composition of the management, did it reflect that same relationship amongst the ethnic groups in the factory and in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because the management of Vitezit, at least the part that I worked in, you had a Croat and a Serb and a Muslim working together in the top management, and in the production of explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Nusret Kalco at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the management board for outer chemical activities. He was a machine engineer and he worked in all spheres outside the chemical industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nusret Kalco was a Muslim by nationality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was he the sole manager of a higher rank who was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No. We had senior managers, that is to say, the director of development was a Muslim and my immediate associate, Mr. Haris Vrbanjac the commercial director, he was a also a Muslim. The director of the transport services, and this as a very large service and large department in view of what Vitezit did, it exported throughout Europe, and the head of that department was Mr. Zukic, he was also Muslim. So those are some of the individuals that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that the events in Bosnia led to a series of problems and that production dropped. But you continued working, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in the course of 1992, you put out certain quantities of the material you were producing. Could you tell us what your markets were, who your buyers were at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I must say that the market for our products, civil engineering explosives, went to mines, mines which are in the Bosniak regions, Tuzla, Zenica, Kakanj and formerly this was Vlasenica, Srebrenica and so on. So there was a need for these products and we wanted to employ the people that we were able to employ and send our products to these regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you had to ship your goods and receive payment for your goods, what was the a situation there, the transport situation and the payment situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, can I divide my answer up into two parts? First, I'd like to mention the mines. Mining companies, and they were our largest beneficiaries, customers, and we -- the producers of explosives in Bosnia-Herzegovina like to receive payment. But when it came to the smaller consumers such as the stone quarries and others, we were guided by the principle that we ship the goods to those who were able to pay up front, regardless of the territory we were sending it out to in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In view of the specific nature of your products, transport was a highly sensitive area as well, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was highly sensitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, in view of the conditions that prevailed in Bosnia and where your customers lay, did you have serious problems in transporting your goods?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We had to ensure the whole chain until -- to our customers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In 1992, you managed to retain some of the market, that is to say, to dispatch your products to the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was that your -- were your shipments regular shipments?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That depended on requirements and on how far the companies from the Republic of Croatia were able to pay for the goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember whether at the beginning of 1993 you still had goods to send to the market?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, we did have some, but from the beginning of 1992, at the beginning of 1992, we saw that due to the aviation and JNA attacks, that for security reasons, safety reasons, we had to move our stockpiles. Because of the safety of the town of Vitez and its environs, first of all, and also to be able to export our goods further afield to the customers that wanted them, to the markets in western Europe and to our market in the Republic of Croatia. The goods were moved to warehouses around the city of Split, that is, in the town of Sinj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that before the war you also had warehouses in the port of Ploca, which was your export port?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vitezit was a large exporter overseas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And now you had more warehouses outside Vitez, and they were in Split and Sinj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As for regular production, would it be true to say that on the 16th of April, 1993 the factory was still operating?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: To a lesser extent, up until the unhappy events in Ahmici, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. factory operated with the stocks we had available and with explosives which did not depend on imported components. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm preparing now paragraph 1.5. I wouldn't repeat it. The witness told us that two days ago. I could only with one question ask the witness whether he agrees with that, yes or no, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It wasn't disputed. The only matter you may want to deal with is the final sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, sir. I'm not receiving the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only matter you may want to deal with -- there's no need to repeat the rest of the paragraph, it hasn't been disputed. The only matter you may want to deal with is the final sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nakic, in the summary we have prepared, in point 1.5, we're referring to the last sentence. Would you tell me, please, in view of the importance of the factory in the technological chain, which was explained earlier, and along with everything you have explained today, can it be said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness give the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain whether the factory was important for any of the forces involved in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you explain that briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I was referring to civil engineering explosives, some of which, to a certain extent, could be important for what was evidently going to happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But part of the former military production, the so-called special purpose production, was very important, and it was to be supposed that all three sides would be interested in taking over that part of the factory. The best proof of this was the aggression of the former JNA. They tried on several occasions to take over, and then they shelled the factory, bombed it, they tried to destroy it. We can assume that the Muslims had the same attitude because of the way their forces were deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were prepared for wartime activities from Vogosca, Konjic, Bugojno, Novi Travnik, the part that they controlled, and it was logical that they would want to take the Vitez factory as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the other side, needed only the gunpowder production in order to have the entire military production they needed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you, in early 1992, start managing your business from Split more and more?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, in early 1992 it was evident that we could not go on working normally, especially the financial and commercial departments which needed to create the conditions for a normal production process. In the search for new sources of supply of raw materials and the collection of payments for goods delivered, these were companies from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, and export in late 1991 to Germany and Austria. So all this had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, when did you open your office, your branch office, in Split?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, activities started in April 1992, and in June we opened an office in Split, the basic task of which was to perform commercial and financial jobs for the Vitezit company, but also for the other companies within the SPS and the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What role did you personally play in that office in Split? Did you travel? Did you stay in Vitez? Did you move? Could you explain that briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was my duty to perform these tasks, and I started by organising the office, finding premises, office space, in Split; negotiating about these premises and furnishing them in the Monter building in Split; negotiating about the renting of warehouses and transferring part of the vehicles which were to distribute goods in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, in view of the fact that Vitezit was the only company specialised in transporting dangerous substances in accordance with international regulations. On our return, in the management we decided that a group of people should be sent to perform all these tasks operatively. Mr. Haris Vrbanjac, he is a Muslim, he was the first to go there. And Mr. Dzevad Redzanovic went with him, also a Muslim, a technologist, in order to demonstrate to our new customers in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, in view of the changed conditions after the breakup of the former Yugoslavia. Two vehicles with four drivers, two of whom were Muslims also, in June 1992 they moved to Split and they started living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At what time did you physically move to Split completely, you personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, throughout this time I used to go to Split, had contacts there, but I moved in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From time to time you travelled between Vitez and Split; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us in the autumn of 1992, what did a trip by car from Vitez to Split look like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you that there were several different routes, but I cannot say that any one of them was comfortable, was easy, normal, and safe for a journey from Vitez to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, before the beginning of the war, in the late 1980s, how long would it take you to go from Vitez to Split by car?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: From Vitez to Split, well, in view of the conditions, the car I had, it would be four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In 1992 how long would it take you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, between ten -- there were ten hours or more depending on which checkpoints you would come across and how long they would keep you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about barricades, are you referring to various checkpoints on the route?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And these were checkpoints by all the armies organised in Bosnia at the time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Croatian, Bosniak. Unfortunately, we could not even pass through Serbian territory at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You nowhere passed through territory controlled by the JNA or the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In fact, there was a road called the Road of Salvation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was its aim?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, the Road of Salvation - I took a direct part in its construction - it was built by the Croats and the Muslims together. The only purpose was to create the conditions for normal supplies both for Croats and for Muslims so that they would survive. I am talking about food, most of all, and the basic necessities of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So as not to waste time on this road, just one more question about it. This road which the municipalities from Central Bosnia built with their own resources was meant to bypass certain Serb-controlled areas in order to open up communication toward the south; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And for you from Central Bosnia, was it the only way to go toward the south?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the only road to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You explained what the office did, the office in Split. To conclude this part of my questioning, when did that office start engaging in other activities other than business?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, we can say that from the time it was founded the office performed certain other activities, and I will tell you why. In 1992, in April, after the first shelling by the JNA and the aviation, there was an exodus of women and children from Vitez. Most of them ended up in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, from Makarska to Zadar and further north. The part of the population which stayed closer to Vitez -- sorry, I meant Split, used the office as a kind of centre where they could gather, get information, ask for advice, get assistance, especially women; for those who could not get hold of money, who were not familiar with those surroundings and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can all this be described by saying that a good part of your job was to provide welfare to your citizens from Central Bosnia, that you were a kind of consular office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In 1993 at some point, these relations started being formalised because this used a lot of resources; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have one document which is really very short, unfortunately not translated because this one came with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And of course I did give a copy to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nakic, would you please take a look at this document which you gave me, and would you explain the significance of this document? It mentions your name. Can you tell us what it's about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of the events in Central Bosnia and the problems that were evident, the civilian authorities decided that -- well, in this document, they are simply listing the names of the people from the Vitez municipality who were officially to take over certain tasks in organising assistance for people who happened to be on the territory of Republic of Croatia and also to provide assistance to the territory of the Vitez municipality. Because of the closing of all communications, it was no longer possible to come and go, and that is why an office was established on the premises of the Vitezit office which now extended its activities to perform certain jobs which I have already described, mainly to provide help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just tell us in a few words what the document is, will you please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you just say who issued it and what it says?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was issued by the mayor, by the president of the municipality of Vitez, Mr. Ivan Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And perhaps for the sake of translation, so we can understand it fully, you could read the last paragraph at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: "The task of this office is to organise all kinds of help for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. municipality of Vitez with continuous cooperation, contacts by fax and telephone with members of the HVO government in Vitez, with members of the civilian authorities of the municipality of Vitez," in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much,. I would like to adduce this document -- to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document D114/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now we'll get a translation of this quickly, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's already ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little later, sometime in summer, other Central Bosnian municipalities with the HVO in power in one way or the other joined and used the same infrastructure, rather those warehouses and the personnel that you had set up in Split; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will now show you this document. Will the usher please help me distribute it. Will you please have a look at this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document D115/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nakic, is it correct that this document is about that period of time and that situation when you expanded your services to cover also other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I should say the activities and the need to help people who were in the encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So far in your testimony today, you mentioned the vehicles that you had in Split so as to distribute your products, your ware. Could you tell us what happened to those vehicles or at least some of them sometime in mid-1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Vehicles were not in Split only, those were vehicles that were found on that unfortunate 16th of April in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. That is, what we were using were two vehicles and others were -- had either gone to bring humanitarian relief or food, that is not only Split but also in Ploce, some in Zadar and even in Zagreb. Those vehicles were, for a while, as I was trying to bring all those people, to concentrate all those people in one place, and in spite of our good business relation -- owing to our good relations with the port of Ploce and our contracts after all, they were put up in the port of Ploce. And so these vehicles and that ware was kept in the port of Ploce, but I learned one day that they had been transported to Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is the territory of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you notify the management of the factory and the municipal authorities, that is Mr. Santic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I notified the company management that the vehicles had been transferred and that I had lost trace of them. As the person in charge, I had to see to it -- to see to the safety of the merchandise of the goods in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have another document shown, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document D116/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, will you cast a look at this document, please, and tell us if the event mentioned here is about that particular incident that you told us about, that is, that those vehicles had been seized by the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Although the text does not show it clearly, it only mentions the military police in Grude, but whose military police was it? What side did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: The Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the HVO military police in Grude seized the vehicles which were the property of your company in Vitez; is that it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Grude is geographically the territory of what state?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is the part of Bosnia called Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this signature here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Head of the municipal council, municipal government, Mr. Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nakic, could you tell us when exactly in 1993, after the war broke out, any land communication was cut off between Vitez and surrounding municipalities towards -- southward, that is, towards Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was at that time of those unfortunate clashes between Croats and Muslims in Central Bosnia, or specifically, in mid-April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what were you asked to do in Split? What were you asked to do to enable at least the transport of the wounded and other patients from the area of Vitez towards Split?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: During that first month of those developments, and I must say that to me it all came as a big surprise, contacts continued primarily to help those who had found themselves in Split. But as the fighting in Central Bosnia gained in intensity and the -- and as the Croat area there was getting smaller by the day because of the encirclement, then the need to somehow inform the outside world, and especially the Republic of Croatia and Europe via contacts with our migrant workers in Europe and so on and so forth. So the purpose of that activity at that time was to communicate the truth about the developments and everything that was going on in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, do go on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: When the first major fighting broke out and when the number of casualties began to increase, of course it became ever more important to help those people who could not be helped at the makeshift hospital in Nova Bila. And it also became necessary to try to devise a solution to use the only way possible, that is, the aircraft to evacuate those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And what was your specific task?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, the specific tasks at that time, on the basis of the information that I had from Vitez and presumably in agreement with UNPROFOR in Central Bosnia, was to try to organise humanitarian medical flights to pull out those people who were in greatest need of help. And then together with representatives - although, yes, I was the coordinator at the time for the municipalities concerned - with representatives of other municipalities we conducted talks, and we also talked to the command of the air base at Divulje in Split, and there we considered the possibilities of sending some helicopters to evacuate the wounded from the area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But let us first try to clarify something so as not to go back to it again. Was this task given to you by the civilian authorities in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: All my contacts throughout my work there, until my return to Vitez, were only and exclusively with representatives of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who were the actors in the organisation of those flights?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: In the territory of Split, I have already said it was the office of the Central Bosnian municipalities, the command, and the operators at the air base at Divulje, and ECMM's EC monitors who checked every approved flight. They checked the helicopter and the contents of what we were sending over there, and I guess there must be documentation to corroborate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Does that mean that helicopters for those flights were supplied by the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Every such flight, the ECMM went through every such helicopter before it took off from Divulje, from Split to Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As a rule, those flights were organised upon receiving calls from Nova Bila Hospital; is that it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And they had permission to fly from the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since you took part in that information chain, did the Croatian authorities, that is, the Croatian army, the Croatian air force, or anyone else, ever authorise any flight without having received previously the document from the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No. Since I invariably was present at all the take-offs and participated in talks with the ECMM representatives, there was not a single flight between July, until the end of August that left the base at Divulje without representatives and European Monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it also an explicit request of the command of the Croatian air force in Split?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about how things were organised at the other end, in Vitez? Was UNPROFOR involved on that side, or wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I believe so, because no flight, no announcement for the evacuation of the wounded was done without the knowledge of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, just a couple of sentences, since you just mentioned it briefly. In real life, what did it look like? Would you describe a flight to us? How did you get the information? Would you be physically present at the take-off? What did the ECMM representative do? And the whole procedure.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: As I have said, I mostly had contact with representatives of the civilian authority, and I presume that they also were in direct contact with the hospital, with the medical personnel who knew who could be helped and who could not, who needed to be transported and who did not. So that part of the procedure would be agreed upon with UNPROFOR, and then they would call us. They would telephone to us and ask us to organise the flight for the transport of the wounded. Unfortunately, it involved usually considerable numbers of people. Such flights were never organised for individuals. So after that I would go to the commander of the air base at Divulje, and together with me he would then get in touch with the ECMM representatives. They would agree on the time of the flight and the day of the flight. That day, before the take-off, together with people involved -- and by this I mean primarily pilots who were to take the steering wheel of the helicopters, so I would see them to it, I would say good-bye to them. Then the ECMM people would board the helicopter, search it, see what there was on board and then would authorise the flight; that is, they would sign the relevant documents authorising the normal take-off. I would stay at the base throughout that time, because from the air base at Divulje to the completion of the flight, that is, until the return of the flight, I would stay at the base there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did the helicopter always take some freight to Vitez and other municipalities, or did it vary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it varied. It depended on circumstances. If we did, yes, they would -- as a rule, if they took anything, then it would be medical supplies, very small quantities, that is, only those which were urgently needed; rather, I should say not as much as the hospital required, but on the basis of what some individuals had ordered, or some medicines which could not be found in the area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In that organisation at that time, while the Croatian army was supplying that helicopter, were any military supplies sent, such as materiel, ammunition, or anything like that, weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever try to do that, at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No, because we had been sternly admonished by both the air base commander and the ECMM representatives about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, pursuant to all the rules and regulations that, at the time, existed in Split and other places, were such operations considered lawful?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What markings did those helicopters have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: They had the red cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What colour were they painted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I believe it was grey, greyish-green, something. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they have any visible HV markings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the only marking was the red cross.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, a red cross and a large white circle so that it could be easily identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that this went on until the end of July 1993. What happened next? Why did it not function after that date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Up until the middle of July, this was intensive; but in the first half of August, flights became less frequent and they were to be discontinued completely after that. Unfortunately, this occurred when the need to pull out the wounded was greatest, and to extend assistance to the unfortunate people in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The aviation command of the HVO, did they tell you of that? Did they inform you of that fact? And if so, how did they do so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, not officially. But in conversations with the staff of the command, they told us the following: that is to say, that those flights were becoming extremely dangerous, that's what they told us, and that the front lines and that the encirclement in Central Bosnia, parts of Vitez, that is, and parts of the Travnik municipality and Novi Travnik municipality, were so narrow that they were no longer safe, and that there was no possibility of helicopters landing safely in those areas and pulling out the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you understand this to be exclusively for safety reasons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time I was not able to understand that or to accept it. Because I had brothers and sisters, and my mother was in Vitez, I had my extended family there, so that for me personally there was no justification for stopping the flights. I was persistent, because what the people told us who had flown, that is to say, the pilots, the crew, they said that they were ready and willing to extend their assistance, to do what they could to help, because probably they had been witnesses to what was going on up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the cessation of these flights, the HV Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. helicopters, that they stopped when the situation grew critical. Did you seek another solution?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The demands by the civilian authorities, and also the demands coming to us from the hospitals and medical staff were such that we had to seek a way of getting the sick and wounded out and to extend the necessary assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that at that time you found a helicopter base which was in Grude first of all, and later on in Posusje, in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received information of that kind, and I personally went to check it out, to see that the information was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The two places you mentioned, they are in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You started discussions with them. What were the conditions? What did you ask them and what were the decisions that were taken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: We had contacts with people who knew the situation, who knew this kind of job. All we knew was that helicopters existed. All the other details we were told to determine for ourselves; that is to say, it was up to us to find the crews for the flights. Because in discussions with the command, there were no relations, no ties anymore, and the people had done these flights either for professional reasons, or they were given other assignments to do in the Republic of Croatia. And new fronts were opened in Croatia as well, new battlefronts. So we had to seek solutions outside those areas, outside Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, we've had a very great deal of evidence in this case. It would be very helpful if you would just tell us shortly what happened. What was the arrangement you made, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On the basis of the information we received, we organised trips to Bratislava and had discussions there with individuals who were to ensure pilots, crews. Whether they were Ukrainians or Russians, I don't really know to this day who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The helicopters that you mentioned in Grude and Posusje, they were helicopters under HVO control, were they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: They were on the territory of Herzegovina and had the Red Cross emblem. I did not actually know who they belonged to, under whose control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you were told to find the crews yourselves, this was an area that you were not acquainted with, so what did you do? This was quite new to you, you didn't have any contacts in that area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This was a new area, and when you undertake a new job you usually look for people who were better acquainted with that area of endeavour than you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, we organised contacts with a man who organised tourist flights by helicopter and who had certain ties to people in the business in -- during peacetime so we contacted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that resulted in the engagement of Russian pilots; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't know whether they were Russian or Ukrainian but they were from the former Soviet Union; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would introduce a couple of documents one set of documents that related to that part of the testimony. [Interpretation] In each of the sets, there are several documents linked to the involvement of the Russian pilots that have just been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it matter whether the pilots were Russians or who they were?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my case is, since we have heard a lot about helicopters and as far as I checked, nobody in any occasion was able to confirm that those were HV helicopters flying over Vitez. And I'm trying to show here that those helicopters were contracted on a more or less commercial base. Indeed we had, as you saw, two different situations on the beginning HV helicopters as a legal performance and we are now on the second part where HV are from middle Bosnia by the performance of this Witness contracted the helicopters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a number for the exhibits together please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These exhibits are D117/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I am going to draw your attention to just some of these documents, not take up too much time, Mr. Nakic. First of all, we have copies of some payments made, payment slips. You don't have to take your originals out, you have them on the table in front of you. English is first followed by the B/C/S. Now these payment slips, we have two and three copies. What are these payment slips, what do they represent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this evidence going to be disputed, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't say it's going to be disputed because I've only just seen it, but it doesn't seem to be exactly critical to the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can see the documents and I can ask questions about them if I want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can see that the documents are a number of payment slips. We can see the names of the payee in each case. Then we've got some other documents if you want to deal with those, but deal with them briefly, please, because we can read what the documents say. To assist you, there seem to be some other claims for expenses. There's a document or some documents of travel expenses for pilots showing them going to Moscow and Budapest. The documents speak for themselves, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I absolutely agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Rather than go through them, unless you want to ask the witness anything particular about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Only one question on the last document, travel authorisation to see -- because that is practically the beginning of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nakic, will you take a look at this document entitled "Travel Authorisation", it is the last document in the set. Tell us please, these gentlemen who were given the assignment to travel, are they the people that you sent to Bratislava, who you sent to check out the crew and determine upon a crew?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature. That was the first time we went for -- to have discussions about bringing in foreign pilots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is an error in transcript on page 26 line 10. There is HV written down instead of HVO. That is where witness mentioned that this territory HVO was in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nakic, these then are documents which indicate the presence of Russian crews; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who financed all this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: All the activities of the department of the office was financed by the municipalities of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nakic, how long did the flights go on with this group of pilots?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: With the first group of pilots, until the end of October 1993. The arrangements went on until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As opposed to the first flights that we discussed with the HV helicopters, these flights were illegal and secret with respect to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, partially illegal because they were mostly from the area of Herzegovina towards Vitez, and only in exceptional cases, when the need arose for very seriously wounded people for them to be transferred to the hospital in Split, we did not give any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that when the flights took the wounded to the hospital in Split, only then did they enter that region?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. If the wounded person was not able to be transported by a vehicle of some other kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you also sent, by means of these flights, various products, just say yes or no. Did you take food?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they take medicines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they take materiel for purposes of the army from time to time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And how did you organise the transport of this material from your warehouses in Split and Ploce to the place from which the helicopters took off which was in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, all the material would be purchased in Herzegovina mostly and in Croatia and then taken by passenger car to the areas in question, to Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is to say, between the boundaries of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was no customs control at the border crossing, was there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And finally, one more question: Can you tell us how frequent those flights were up until October 1993? Give us an idea, was that once a week, several times a day, once a day? What was the average number of flights?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, as there had been no flights for a month and a half with Croat pilots and the foreign pilots, we needed more frequent flying. So there might have been, say, two flights a week, two or three flights a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you were there, as you were in Split and as you looked into the situation there, did you think that the Croatian government would not allow you to transport material from Croatia towards Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you never asked for that, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No. We had a number of contacts in the sense of discussions, that is to say, why the flights had ceased, and it was my impression that Croatia would not have allowed them to take place, the planes to leave from Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did the flights stop once and for all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: This was in January or February 1993. In January, I sent off a second group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It must be 1994.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: 1994. Yes, 1994. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was then that you started organising road convoys for the delivery of aid?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Activities of this kind started much earlier. Together with the Muslim side, we sent a joint convoy in the direction of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of that convoy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: It was later called the "White Road", and it was done in December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was that the first road convoy transporting large quantities of humanitarian aid to the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And finally, since you are here, would you tell us whether you know Mario Cerkez from before the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know him from the company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, because we worked in the same company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to be in ethnically mixed company with him ever?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever notice that he had a negative attitude toward people of another ethnic background for the simple reason that -- for that reason?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No, because he even worked where there were mostly Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Nakic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Kordic has no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will try and be brief because I know there are a number of witnesses we have this week, but this witness has covered quite a lot of territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, just first of all, were you -- in April of 1992, you were still in Vitez, I think.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you present at a meeting in April of 1992, do you remember such meetings involving HVO members of one kind and another?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I was not present at any meetings because I was neither a military organisation or a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that stage, would you qualify for the description of the deputy director of Vitezit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember a decision being made or attempting to be made that the BiH army in Vitez should come under the control of the HVO in the same way as it had done in Mostar? Do you remember that decision being discussed at a meeting at which you were present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I was not at the meeting. I should say that. And secondly, I do not know that there is any document that was issued about the Muslims having to obey the orders of the HVO in Vitez. And the best confirmation of this is that the number of employees up to the highest level in the company where I worked, people who made decisions, even about the distribution of goods, which I have to say is a very sensitive issue, they were Muslims doing those jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've had evidence in this court that for example in October of 1992, Witness G, for reference of the Court, in October of 1992, the security staff at the factory, the Muslim security staff were replaced by military personnel. Do you remember that happening and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it didn't happen because I said -- well, my colleague for example, Nusret Kalco, up until the last day, the unhappy conflict in Ahmici, he was at the factory and he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There may be one or two people in comparatively unimportant positions, but the majority were replaced by the end of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you. People cannot be in one of the leading positions of the management, they cannot be at the head of the warehouse and be considered unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember a visit to your factory by a Croatian General, Praljak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember the Croatian flag being flown at your factory in honour of an important guest or visitor? And if so, why did that happen? Help us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Possible, is it, that that sort of thing would have happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, because we kept in mind, on the basis of our long years of experience and coexistence in Central Bosnia, we wanted to preserve peace on the one hand; and on the other hand, it was in the interests of the Vitezit to have customers. Over 75 per cent of our market is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence that the production of the factory was right run down, was very substantially run down, and there were very substantial cuts in the workforce by November/December 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: In fact, if I may add, the drop in production began a lot earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Coming to 1993, when was it that you removed yourself to Split?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: In October 1993 -- 1992, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said that you came back from time to time from Split. With what frequency did you come back in the period before the outbreak of fighting in April?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately, every 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the police taking over functions within the factory of a security nature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of an incident at the factory involving the raising, probably first, of a Muslim flag and then at the insistence of someone, of a Croatian flag? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move to the 16th of April itself. By then you were -- on that day you were in Split; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that your business there was part business and part welfare; is that really right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Until April 1993, it was mostly business with occasional humanitarian or consular activities, and only for the needs of Vitezit mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just stick with the business for the 16th of April. On that day there were a number of Vitezit lorries in Split; yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: On the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some of them driven by Croat drivers and some of them driven by Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the Croat drivers approached you and obtained from you permission in one way or another to drive their tractors back to Vitez, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They certainly drove back to Vitez, the Croat drivers.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No, because all communications from Vitez were cut, and all the vehicles, as I said, were in the port of Ploca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were the only Dragan Nakic representing Vitezit in Split at that time, weren't you? There wasn't anybody else by that name.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Muslim drivers approached you separately and sought your help, didn't they? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I remember very well. They were not the only ones asking for my assistance. I put them all up in the hotel in Ploca. And over the next few months, in accordance with my activities, I gave everyone assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must challenge that and I must suggest to you that what you did was you demanded from the Muslims drivers the keys to their lorries, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you offered and gave them no assistance of any kind whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. I did not ask for the keys. I visited all the drivers every week in the port of Ploca, and I had regular contacts with them. I passed on the information I had about the events in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've nearly finished this topic. But for witness protection reasons, or potential witness protection reasons, can I just have one minute in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, we're going to adjourn now for half an hour. Would you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence and not to let anybody speak to you about it. Would you be back, please, at twenty-five to twelve.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, after April 16th, did you -- and between then and the end of 1993, did you return at all to Vitez or did you stay permanently in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I've been in Croatia all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you kept informed of what was happening at the factory? Presumably it would be necessary for you to be informed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: To a certain extent, yes, as much as my work and my immediate superior required of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were working as a civilian or as a what in Split?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Only as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who paid you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, since we had our account in Split, because most companies had their non-resident accounts in Split, I was being paid from the account of my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'm going to leap forward to deal with one aspect of the helicopter business. When we're dealing with money, are you saying that you paid real currency to the state of Croatia for the use of their helicopters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: We did not pay anything to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They provided the helicopters free.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While I'm looking for -- you spoke in paragraph 2.6 of your summary of financing the flights. What did you mean then by "financing the flights"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: It is the financing of flights after we hired foreign crews and helicopters from outside the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying that you hired, still staying with money, that you actually paid money for the hire of those helicopters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: In our contract with individuals that we were hiring, these things were stipulated quite clearly, what expenses would be borne by us for the hire of the helicopter and a foreign crew, rather pilots. Who flew from --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just sticking with this and very quickly, who was this foreign body or foreign company that provided helicopters, point number one; and have you got any document showing the payment of money to this body for the hire of the helicopter, point two?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat what I said in my statement, that those were individuals from the territory of the Republic of Croatia whom I met and who directed me. In one of the attachments, there is a document showing who that person is who had contracted the whole business so that in that part of it, I really had no need to go into details except to provide the financing agreement with what had been agreed but there were -- and there is no written trace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying that this little clip of documents produced D119, is it, 117/2 actually contains the cost of hiring the helicopters or does this only deal with hiring the pilots, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: These documents bear only on the hire of pilots and their names are listed here too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back to the original question, it's quite simple: Did you pay money for the hire of helicopters? If so, to whom? I've only gone through those documents very quickly, but I haven't yet picked up the hire of a helicopter. So did you pay money for the hire of helicopters? If so, to whom?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: We provided the money and paid to the individual who arranged the whole deal, although I must say that it was a person who tried to do it as cheaply as possible in order to help the people of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you didn't pay the money to the person who hired you the helicopter, tell us this: Who was it who owned the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that mean you don't know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to take that aspect any further in the time available. From what you learnt of what was happening at your factory following the run-down in production at the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, would you agree with this assessment of the position after April: that after April of 1993, the Vitez HVO government applied itself to reviving military production in the SPS and Vitezit factories? Would you agree with that assessment of that part of the history?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No, as there were no conditions needed to revive the military production, because all the production material had already -- semi-manufacturers had stopped arriving in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you agree that responsibility for organising production lay with the Travnik defence administration, headed by Anto Puljic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What role did Anto Puljic have in relation to the production of materials at the SPS and Vitezit factories?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that because I was keeping in touch only with the management of the company and the civilian authorities in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it right that a number of the expert staff of the factory had been forced to go to the front lines, and that production at the factory was left in the hands of less experienced operatives?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, everybody had to go to the front line because of the situation in Central Bosnia and the encirclement. There were very, very few people, so that there was no choice but to send everybody to the front, from 16 to the age of 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Did that have the effect of leaving less experienced people dealing with production?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I really know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know two businessmen by the name of Miroslav Sukic, or Sucic, I think it probably should be, and Branko Mlakic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Milan Sucic, yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: And Branko Nakic [as interpreted], no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that first name associated with production at the factory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And after, or during and after?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Not during the war because he was not in Vitez; and after the war he spent about a year in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with products at the factory.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May he have been involved in the production of the factory in the period of time leading up to February of 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How do you know that? You didn't seem to know very much, but how do you know he wasn't? May he have been involved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I know that because the man lived and worked in Zagreb. His family was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just deal with the helicopters now. In June of 1993, was there anyone apart from you in Croatia dealing with the movement of helicopters to Central Bosnia, so far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: What I know is that these were the only flights to Central Bosnia from the air force base at Divulje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've had evidence in relation to June of 1993 of the discovery of helicopters carrying ammunition and unused Croatian dinars. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The references, for the Court, are the witness Brix-Andersen and Exhibits 1012 and 1017.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you know about helicopter flights carrying ammunition and Croatian dinars, please, if you were the only person dealing with such flights?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I know absolutely nothing about that flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that you were dealing just with humanitarian issues, is that right, from your end?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: In the first part and at the time when those were the flights from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, that is, from the air force base at Divulje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were sending helicopters off to bring back military wounded; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: People who had been severely wounded and who could not be administered proper medical help at the makeshift hospital in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Soldiers who had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Civilians, soldiers, all those who needed medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So part of your function, at the very least, was in respect of military personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The factory at the time was under HVO/military control, wasn't it? It had to be in time of war.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I have pointed out already that I was there primarily because of the product mix concerning the civilian part of the production, and that was my primary task. I really was in no position to discuss any military part, or to even know particulars or details about the military production in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you telling us, so that we understand it, that even from April of 1993, there was serious production of equipment and materials at the SPS factory for non-military purposes? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I have already said both military and non-military. In view of the fact that we were engaged in a highly specific production, that over 90 per cent were imported semi-manufactured, then simply there were no conditions to organise any production.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just so that we understand it, what non-military production and for what non-military customers was the SPS factory producing equipment after April of 1993 and before December of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat it once again. There was no production. Non-military, I mean all the civilian explosives for civilians uses and polyethylene packaging based on PVC, combatory products, machine tools and all that, and I won't list everything because the SPS was a major plant which before the war employed over 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on. In July of 1993, Mr. Nakic, we've had evidence - I believe with Witness AD and another witness, I'm not sure whether he was protected or not, at pages 15.957 and onwards - we've had evidence in June or July of 1993 of helicopters landing in the quarry behind Vitez close to the ammunition factory. Did you understand that to be the place where your helicopters were going to land?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that was the best choice from the point of view of safety, not because of the vicinity of the plant there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that they were discharging weapons and ammunition, did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I have already said that the helicopters which took off from the air base at Divulje and those which we were sending with the knowledge of the ECMM were never engaged in the transport of any weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 18th of July, Darko Gelic told -- gave information and it's Exhibit 1146.2, that a helicopter flight was bringing some very -- some piece of very important equipment. Now, you say in paragraph 2.5 of your summary, and you said in evidence, that these helicopters brought technical assets for military purposes. Does that mean weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And today, I'm reminded, you used the phrase "equipment for the purposes of the army. "

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But the helicopters which had been hired and engaged, that was the end of 1993 when the situation was extremely hard and complex. The number of wounded, of dead, was growing with every day and the possibilities for defence were ever lesser. And the only message from Vitez was to send any kind of help, and that included materiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, can I have an answer to the question, please? When you use in your summary one phrase, and when you spoke today of equipment for the purposes of the army, was that a phrase that covered weapons? Were these helicopters bringing in weapons, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what about July of 1993 when it was the Croatian helicopters that were not charging you for their use, what were they doing? Bringing in weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Only, and only medical supplies and again, based on individual orders and requests because they were not in supply at the pharmacy in Nova Bila with the only and exclusive goal to evacuate wounded, those who could be helped only outside the hospital at Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you left -- or sorry, not when you, when the helicopters left Split, they were under some kind of supervision from the International Community, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But would this be right, Witness Z is the relevant witness, would this be right, that, in fact, the helicopters flew below the radar zone and they weren't detectable and therefore, you couldn't tell whether they put down and picked up some more equipment later on after they left Split. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I really cannot answer that because I'm not an aviation expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see that -- we've had evidence and it's -- Your Honour, it's the same witness -- that later on in March of 1994, an incident happened at Nova Bila with a helicopter. Were you in Nova Bila in March of 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
