utterances.text: No. I came in Vitez in late April of 1993 [as interpreted], but not by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I thought, unless I've got it entirely wrong, that you were in Croatia from April 1993 until the end of the year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: From October 1993 until April 1994, until the end of April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, therefore, an incident at the end of 1994 would be an incident that you would hear about or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I have not heard about such an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would be a helicopter that you would have sent, if it was a -- one of your helicopters -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, I really hate it but there is substantial error in transcript, page 46 line two, there should be the year 1994. The date when witness returning. He said so clearly. It could dramatically change the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You see we've had evidence here from Peter Williams and Witness Z of a helicopter that landed illegally in Nova Bila on the 11th of March of 1994. Well that must be a helicopter sent by you, mustn't it? It was a medivac flight?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: In my statement, I already said when the overland routes were opened, these activities stopped, and that was already January, February, 1994 when we stopped hiring helicopters. So that the testimony of March 1994 and all that, about the helicopter then, I really know nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, help us, please. If not you, because you've been doing all the welfare work so you tell us, and you were still there, and this is a medivac helicopter, if it wasn't you, who did send it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: May I just point out, Your Honour, that the indictment for my client is until September 1993. I don't see any relevance of what going on in -- with the new helicopters probably in April 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's all part of the story. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last question on this, Mr. Nakic. You see, we have had evidence that that helicopter had 20 soldiers with new uniforms carrying bags and boxes and that they got out of the helicopter and that the International Community representatives had to send them back. Now, did you really not hear about this? Now, you were in Split organising the distribution of aid. Did you really not hear about this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I really didn't hear about that, and I've already said that as far as the activities on the white road are concerned and with the opening up of road traffic, our activities and gentlemen, the available resources that were limited, represented an end for our mission of bringing in humanitarian aid by air.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, one last question on helicopters apart from the way they'll turn up in some documents we'll have a look at, and then I'll be done. I suppose you learned about the hijacking of the Muslims' medivac helicopters, didn't you, in October of 1993? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nor about their detention for five months although they were apparently engaged on humanitarian work. You didn't hear a word about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we just look at a few documents. Some new, most of them existing. If Your Honour will just give me one minute. I'd like please -- just have a quick look at a new document, 1198.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm primarily concerned here with your evidence about the factory and what it was doing, do you understand? This is a document of the 10th of September, 1993, from the Travnik defence department to Bruno Stoic, and it's signed by Anto Puljic. It's a request to safeguard the helicopter flights between Kiseljak and Busovaca. Do you know anything about those helicopter flights?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see a document of this kind; I really cannot tell you anything about it. Nor with regard to the safeguarding of the flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you've talked about helicopters, and we know at this time that helicopters were provided by Croatia. It's right, isn't it, that the HVO didn't have its own helicopters; that's why Croatia was providing them. I don't think you need to look at the document for this. Just help us, Mr. Nakic. It's right, isn't it, that the HVO didn't have helicopters; that's why Croatia was providing them, and that's why you tell us that you had to hire other ones at a later date.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this is a document which dates back to September --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just wait for Their Honours. Sorry to interrupt you. If you would like now to give the answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: This is a document which dates back to September, and Croatian helicopters flew at the end of June, July, which means in the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you were still dealing with helicopter flights. If the HVO had access to helicopter flights in September of 1993, who was providing the helicopters? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether the HVO had them or not, and who assured them. I only know the part of the business that I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The third paragraph of this document: "We have a small number of jackets for 60-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortar shells. We can fill them in Vitez." That's right, isn't it? There was a capability in your factory in September 1993 to produce mortars.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat once again that with respect to this military aspect, as I spent my entire lifetime working in production, the production of explosives for civil engineering, and this was substantially different from the military section, that I really don't know anything about these military matters and details. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document 1215.2, please. A new document, a milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say the frequency of your flights to Croatia was, please, Mr. Nakic? One a week, one a month, one a day, two a day? What?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, from Croatia there might have been one in seven or ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: They were relatively infrequent. A small number of flights from the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd like to look at this document, I'm afraid -- maybe you speak English, from what I heard you say earlier, but it's only an English version document. It will be laid on the ELMO. It's a military information summary from one of the international military units there. In paragraph 3, it deals with helicopter activity, and it reads, I'll read it slowly and ask your comment: "Croat helicopter activity in contravention of the no fly zone has continued with two flights recorded today," and their times are given. "On both occasions the landing site was again the quarry at Mosunj, and the helicopter employed the spiralling technique recently noted to gain and lose height within the safety of Croat controlled valley base ..." I think just a tiny detail. The spiralling technique is where the helicopter drops very rapidly, almost like a stone, to the ground in order to get down quickly; that's correct, isn't it? Mr. Nakic, that's correct, isn't it? That's the spiralling technique. You know about that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know what time we're talking about here, what period. And knowing the terrain, because I was born there, and on the basis of the information and contacts with my brothers and my mother there, as far as how near -- I knew that the lines were near, then it is logical that the helicopter was only able to use the spiralling technique to lose height and to land. In view of the fact that Muslim activities were strong along those lines, according to the information that my relatives sent to me, there was no other choice, there was no other possibility but to use this technique.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. But as to two flights in one day, could they both be yours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I said that I don't know the period that this refers to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: -- so I can't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 26th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: It is possible at that time; that is to say, from the 20th we engaged foreign pilots. So it is possible that there were two flights in one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same paragraph records a little bit further down: "Seven flights in the previous week." Could those be all your flights?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I assume that they were. From the documents that I have in front of me, I think that the flights started sometime around the 20th with foreign crews, foreign pilots. And as I said earlier on, in view of the cessation of communication with Central Bosnia, then it was logical that it was necessary to intensify the number of flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have a quick look at one other document, 1225.1, which is another military information summary, and this suggests -- well, we'll have a look at it very quickly. You'll see that this document relates to the period up until the 30th of September, and it speaks here under the paragraph headed "Vitez," it deals with the landing of a helicopter in the quarry. But if we look at the comment, it says: "Today's helicopter activity takes the running total to ten flights in ten days." Now, were these all the private flights you were funding out of SPS money?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: It was the -- if it's the end of September, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because the same military information summary suggests that "Local Croat sources have claimed that the helicopter brings in munitions and takes out people for a price"; correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that is correct, because I know for certain that we took a lot of people who were volunteers, and they were working in many European countries. So that I did not have an opportunity to see or hear that anybody was taken out for a price.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In any event, by this week, that is, the week ending the 30th of September, it was, so far as you were concerned, only the private helicopters that were operating; is that right? No more Croatian helicopters.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can he please have a look at 1223.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is one day before the summary contained in that last report; this is the 29th of September, 1993. Now, if you look at this document, this document comes from the defence department for Travnik, it goes to the office of the vice-president of the republic in Mostar, and it's an operative report that says this: "During the past 24 hours in the territory of Central Bosnia, Travnik municipality, Novi Travnik, Vitez and Busovaca, we noticed the following: 1. The municipal centres of the MiO, as well as lookout networks on the field, did not register the flight of enemy helicopters or other low-flying aircraft. An HV helicopter landed securely, regardless of strong fire opened by MOS forces." Now, thinking back, what about this Croatian helicopter, please, in the period where you say it was just private helicopters? Is this one of yours or somebody else's? The Court will see it's also referred to at the foot of the first page in paragraph 2. Can you explain, please, the landing of Croatian helicopters at the time when you say that you were now dependent on private suppliers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I still maintain that those were the only helicopters from the base in Posusje which we organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But does it appear, and do you know anything about the fact that other people were also flying in Croatian helicopters doing things unknown to you? Does that follow, necessarily, from this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I don't think they were doing that because I talked and met pilots from Croatia and they were very sorry that the humanitarian flights had been stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By this time they weren't just humanitarian, were they, Mr. Nakic? By this time you were flying in weapons.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We know from document 1302.2 that in November of 1993, there was an order from Anto Puljic to have a helicopter pad constructed. Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that fit, as it were logically, with the level of helicopter flights that you were organising or would that really not be explained by the level of flights you were organising?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult for me to explain the need for building a helicopter pad in view of the fact that I know the terrain very well and the circumstances that prevailed there at the time of the worst conflicts which was October, November and December of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, the truth is there were a great number of helicopter flights. Some may have been by a private supplier, I'm not in a position to deal with that, and some were by Croatia, and that's why they needed a helicopter pad, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know that they flew -- that is to say, that Croatian helicopters flew and I think -- and I can't tell you anything about the helicopter pad either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your position in Croatia, did you learn of the threats made to blow up your factory in the autumn of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And these were threats not made by the Muslims, these were threats made by Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Correct. But it was a warning to the world that the Croats should be protected and defend themselves because that was all that remained for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They were serious threats, weren't there? There's no question of just being propaganda, they were serious threats.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of the situation that prevailed in the field and that lots of people died every day, all that remained for those people up there to do was to undertake such an action and to warn the world to try and stop the hostilities that were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shan't trouble the witness with 1299.1 and 1305.4 in those circumstances. Can we have two -- three more documents each very short, I think, possibly four. 1324.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's my mistake, Mr. Nakic, entirely, I can't quite understand your function in Croatia. I want you to help me though, through this document. This is a document that goes to Anto Puljic from the factory director, Marko Lujic, and it sets out wartime production plans for the period 6th to the 12th of December. It sets out a lot of military equipment and then at the bottom some stoves, candles, and beds, and boots. Does any of this material or, sorry, is any of this material material in the production of which you had an interest?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: First of all, these are materials, the production of which I have -- I can say nothing about. Let me remind you that in Split at the branch office there, and this is quite logical, an office was set up for a civilian programme for the placement and work of civilian programmes because military production wasn't ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But to save time there was no civilian production. This is what your factory was producing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was no civilian production and your only function in Split appears to have been to send helicopters. Would that be --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but by expanding activities, the activities of the office, humanitarian and social welfare for the many wounded who, after being hospitalised, had been left to the streets or to be put and accommodated somewhere. So we had to contact people and family members who were abroad. There were many activities of this kind that we had to see to, so you cannot, via an office that was public in nature and where ten other Muslim companies worked from the territory of the federation, from an office of this kind, you couldn't do any business of this kind nor did I engage in any business of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you got any document that shows your appointment for welfare work, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I think that that document was presented at the beginning of these proceedings and it stated the appointment of the office and the appointment of individuals and it was signed by the mayor, and it was exclusively humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at another document. 1355.4. This is a document that is, in a sense, historical. It says something about the period of time you've been telling us about. It's dated the 8th of January, 1994. It goes from the Travnik defence administration to Franjo Sliskovic personally, he being Blaskic's logistics man, and it's signed by Marko Lujic and it's on the -- the subject is the sending of requests. What it says is this: "During 1993, starting from the 1st of August, we filled with explosives and completed sets of materiel delivered by helicopter. Since the war" -- and this is a draft translation, I suspect, "Since the war production section is closing requests from last year, we ask you to send, as soon as possible, a collective request for all materiel that arrived in this way between the 1st of August and the 31st of December. We also ask you to send your requests this year immediately after the arrival of the materiel in which the war production section has to work." But here he is, Marko Lujic of your factory, saying between August and later, they "filled with explosives and completed sets of materiel delivered by helicopter." Those are your helicopters, aren't they, the ones you sent, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already stressed helicopters, but not 1st of August because in August, they were not there. Up to mid-August it was only the Croatian ones that flew, and they quite certainly were not bearing products of this kind. With the engagement and activities in the second half of September, that is to say, we sent humanitarian aid primarily, and by the end of the year as I said, some materiel resources as well, some materiel. I cannot say whether they were fulfilling purposes or whatever. That business was done via the office by many people and some of them were experts. So I can't really tell you. I can't say what kind of equipment or materiel or weapons were in question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, this letter comes from a person who should know, Marko Lujic and is quite specific about the start date, the 1st of August. Now, you've tied yourself to saying that Croatian helicopters were still flying in that period of August until September. Think back, please. Croatian helicopters, just like any other later helicopters, were flying munitions in to Central Bosnia and that's the truth of it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: From Croatia, from Croatia they could not have flown, and if those helicopters were checked daily by the monitors, by the ECMM, so this date is an incorrect date in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to take that any further with this witness. Perhaps he would like to take a look at his own exhibit, 114/2. I am grateful to Mr. Lopez-Terres for his sharp eyes as ever, and it might be good if he had a look at 116/2 as well, just lay one beside the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see the stamp that we've got here is the defence administration of Travnik, isn't it? It's not the civilian body at all. We haven't got a translation of this document yet, but the stamp is the defence administration, that's who appointed you; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Santic, when we are talking about the document of the 27th of April, I really cannot go into the kind of stamp. I wasn't interested in the kind of stamp because all my contacts throughout this time were, in 90 per cent of the cases, as agreed with Mr. Santic and the representatives of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please help me. We have heard a lot about stamps, the use of stamps in the former Yugoslavia. Is that or is that not the stamp of the defence administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you able to read what it says underneath "Vitez"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: It says "defence administration", but in my view, the person was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour will find that I'm not going to take time but 116/2 the one dealing with the vehicles has the civil administration stamp. The last document, 1364.8.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you know about the Koncar factory, please, Mr. Nakic? What did you know about the Koncar factory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing because we did not have any business dealings with the Koncar factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just look at this document, please, you were still in Split. This is a document dated the 28th of January 1994 from the Travnik defence administration to an assistant minister and various other people, and also to the chief of production administration, Bruno Stoic, signed by Puljic. The subject is a report on final user of goods sent by helicopter. "We inform you that the goods sent by helicopter are intended for the Ministry of Defence for the Republic of Croatia for the Koncar factory and the explosives are there set out in accordance with an earlier agreement." These helicopters weren't just carrying injured people, were they, they were carrying munitions in and sometimes they were carrying munitions out.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I really do not know anything about this document or those relations with Koncar, especially about gunpowder, because I did not work with gunpowder. So I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nakic, just a few details that should be cleared up. Is it correct that from October 1992 on you no longer lived in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You lived in Split; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that from October 1992 until April 1994 -- let us break this down into two time periods. From October 1992 until the outbreak of the conflict, the 16th of April, 1993, you said you went to Vitez from time to time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you said, if I remember correctly, that you went there every 15 days or so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is an average.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I stayed there for a certain time because I had business to do. There were certain activities in the company, talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you consider -- I apologise for speaking too fast. Do you consider that because of these visits lasting a few days you were well informed about what was going on in Vitez at this time, when you were no longer living there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There were questions about the drivers employed in your company. They were accommodated in Ploca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. First in the Ploca Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And certainly these drivers were dissatisfied with their position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for their dissatisfaction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that they were people who had, like all of us, left their families in Vitez, and that was the main reason. Not my attitude toward them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As for these people, you tried to talk to them on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning we had daily contacts, because they used to come to Split from Ploca, one or two of them, and I went there every week. The money I took from the bank account I distributed among those people so they would have something to live on, and there are documents to show this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, these drivers were your employees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There were both Croats and Muslims among them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was your duty to look after your employees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that both the Muslims and the Croats from that group wanted to go home?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was the topic of all your conversations with them.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Most often, yes, and the information that I was able to get by telephone and pass on to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This went on for several months.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let's say it was a few months, because -- because of these unfortunate roadblocks and then the unfortunate events in Ahmici. So up until June, when the encirclement became critical, with the Court's permission, and when large numbers of wounded Croats began arriving from that area and came to the office, then the drivers stopped coming to the office so often. And the contacts became more risky because there were two opposing sides. There were people whose families had been killed, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have information that at one point several Muslim drivers, not all of them, decided on their own initiative to go home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that they wanted to leave with vehicles which were owned by the company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That is correct. And if I can add what I failed to mention when asked by the Prosecutor, the way they asked for the keys. There were two vehicles driven by Mr. Cevan [phoen] and Muslims, they disappeared; the vehicle of Enes Ramic disappeared. And I was given instructions that the vehicles, not the people but the vehicles, should be confiscated and the keys for their safekeeping. No one knows to this day where those vehicles ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, those vehicles were undoubtedly the property of your company.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it your duty to look after the company property?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the end, according to OTP information, they were arrested in Capljina; some of them were anyway. Where is Capljina? On the territory of which state?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything about this previously?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to ask, just for two short questions on those documents which were raised by the Prosecution, for a private conference to mention the names of the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One more short question in this connection. Did you ever in your life, before this situation, have any involvement at all in dealings with helicopters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about this world, the business circles dealing in helicopters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No. I was involved in a completely different branch of industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you employed someone to do this for you, this kind of business?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that that was the man whose name you mentioned, who was an expert in this business.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever directly negotiate with the owners of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these helicopters, whom you found in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1993, is it true that you always had certain products on stock from your factory in warehouses in Ploca, Split, and Sinj?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you sell those products in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, please think carefully. Did you ever, at any time in the period we are discussing, have any involvement in any undertakings regarding helicopters, apart from the two you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, if we are to get through 11 witnesses this week, we really must make progress. This witness has been giving evidence all morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, Your Honour. I will have only two short questions more. I'm just about to finish. May I? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever hear or see, you personally, or did you ever hear from someone that there were other helicopters flying from Divulje to Central Bosnia, apart from the project we mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of the fact that I had a lot to do in the office and in organising this, I really did not inquire, and I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: To give us an idea of the size of this, the numbers, could you tell us what number of wounded you took care of, you and the people from your office, in 1993, in Split; whom you visited in hospital, took things to them, took them out of hospital, took them to other hospitals for rehabilitation? Can you give us an idea of the numbers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that there were between 80 and 100 people in the hospitals all the time. When some were released, others would arrive. I think I even have some documents here about the way these people were received and accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So on average in 1993, this was the number of people in the hospitals.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO NAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have further questions for this witness. But if I may just add one comment in order to avoid any further -- so if you feel, I can then ask. Related to the stamp the Prosecution was talking a lot about, I just wanted to remind you - and that is why I wouldn't ask the witness - that there were two witnesses which in detail explained the division of the government and what was, indeed, the defence office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nakic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a matter for your decision, but I feel that I am obliged just to tell you, to remind you, you have asked us to give you an overview on the status of how we will proceed. Would you like to have that after this witness, or we'll just keep it ready and then advise you as soon as we have some break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have the witness. Let's get on with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I note that this witness will be the 200th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Cerkez's Defence I will examine you. Please answer to the best of your recollection, and please bear in mind that you should speak slowly and pause between my question and your answer so that the interpreters can do their job. And for the record, would you please tell us your full name and your place and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Josip Miskovic born on the 4th of August, 1964 in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You reside in Vitez now.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are married and the father of one, age three.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I got married after the war. I have a little daughter who is three years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: By nationality, you are a Croat, a Roman Catholic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have dual citizenship, Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you graduated from the technical military academy in Zagreb in 1989?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in two or three sentences why and how you studied at the technical military academy? Were you there as a civilian or a military man, and does that school enable people to get a job in the military or can they also get a job in the civilian sector?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I had a grant from the explosives factory in Vitez, Vitezit, so that on completion of the technical military academy, I had a job waiting for me at the factory. After graduating from the academy, I could choose whether to stay in the military or to remain a civilian. I decided to remain a civilian, to go home and to do the job that I had been trained to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Because in the former Yugoslavia, the Vitezit factory was of military significance because of the essentials of its production, it closely cooperated with the then JNA and the military authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you said you decided to remain a civilian and after completing the military academy, you returned to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you got a job in Vitezit, the factory that had given you a grant for your studies.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to try to clarify this. I was given a grant by Vitezit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it's important, somebody will ask you about it, Mr. Miskovic, but we really need to get on to the important matters. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are a graduate engineer in chemical technology?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you are still employed in Vitezit as the director of the development department?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You served in the former JNA in Nis in 1983?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There you had some military training and acquired the rank of reserve lieutenant after you left the JNA, after the academy, after you graduated from the academy then. You have been a member of the HDZ since its founding in Bosnia and Herzegovina but you have no party function?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your address in 1992 was in the village of Kremenjace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The village of Kremenjace is a part of the village of Buhine Kuce?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that, that it's a part of Buhine Kuce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is the ethnic make-up of the population in that village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: The village is mixed. There are Croats and Muslims. It's about 50/50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that after the fall of the town of Jajce, refugees arrived in your area?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And refugees from that territory arrived in your village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Jajce, Kotor Varos, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of the refugees that came to your village from parts of Jajce and Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly the refugees that came to our village when parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina fell were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, you will not find Kremenjace and Buhine Kuce on the map. Is that really Sivrino Selo which is marked on the map? The witness can show it to us if the Court feels it necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I think we know. But it's another village with a series of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's a little bit confusing, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the needs of the Tribunal, we are now coming across various names for the same village. When we talk about Sivrino Selo, the lower part near the road, what was it called?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: We -- well, our village is between two big villages, Santici and Dubravica. Above us is Sivrino Selo. Before the war, we were the local commune of Kremenjace before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that after the fall of Jajce, Muslim refugees came to your village. That fact, did it have any influence on the interethnic relations in the village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, with the arrival of outsiders in our village, certain tensions arose, people started to be afraid of the newcomers who had come to our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Did you notice in late 1992 and in 1993 that the Muslim villages started some activities and the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I noticed in the second half of 1992 they had set up single ethnic group roadblocks. I used to move around a lot. I used to go around a lot, and on my way home, I was always stopped at a checkpoint by unknown people and one local man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims, were they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a Muslim checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that trenches had been dug in your village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: In late 1992 and early 1993, trenches were dug above the Croatian houses in the village; facing our houses, and also around Mr. Sefkija Dzidic's house who was a local man in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ask your fellow villagers why they had dug trenches facing Croatian houses?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we asked them for an explanation because it made us feel unsafe. Why were the trenches facing us? Why weren't they facing the Serbian Chetnik army which we could expect from that direction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And was there explanation realistic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, because the lines toward the Serbian aggressor were on Vlasic and around Turbe up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And if there was a breakthrough by Serb forces from the direction of Vlasic, could this be expected from the direction of the Croatian houses or from the opposite side, from the north-west?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not logical that those forces would come from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And one more question before we have our lunch break. You mentioned that Sefkija Dzidic's house was in your village.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his function was at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that, as far as I can remember, that he was a member of the municipal Crisis Staff, the joint staff that was established in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And later on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, later on I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say that there were trenches around his house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were dug at the same time as the trenches facing our houses, the trenches around his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In 1992, earlier, before this, before this wave of refugees arrived, did you, together with your Muslim neighbours, fortify the village in some way?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Muslims and the Croats in early April 1992, we built a shelter because the air raids had started by the Serb Chetnik forces in Vitez and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have now come to point three Your Honours, so this may be a convenient moment for our lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Miskovic, we are going to adjourn now for the lunch break for an hour and a half. Would you please remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence during that adjournment, and that includes members of the Defence team. Don't speak to anybody until it's over. Could you be back, please, at twenty-five to three. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us move on, Mr. Miskovic. Before we adjourned for lunch, we had come to item 3, that is events of 1993. Let me ask you by way of introduction, Mr. Miskovic, at that time, that is in early 1993, you worked for Vitezit, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Early 1993 are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm saying early 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you had already stopped working at the Vitezit. Is it that there was no work there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I was put on standby in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the eve of the conflict in Vitez and around it, that is on the eve of the 16th of April, you were not in the area of Vitez, you were outside the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when did you come back?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I came back from Split on the 14th of April. 14th of April, I was on my way back from Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And which route did you take?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Split, now the border crossing, I don't know which one, but across Mount Vran, and we got as far as Gornji Vakuf, that is Sebesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when you got to Sebesic, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: We were stopped by armed persons. As we came close, we saw that it was a unit of -- I don't know what they're called, really, but it was a unit, an armed unit -- well, a Croat formation. And we -- they told us that the road towards Vitez was cut off in the next village, in Opara, because the day before that, four Croat commanders had disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me just ask you this. You were in a private car?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We were travelling with two trucks, because I had gone to Split to get the humanitarian relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you were taking Caritas relief from Split to Vitez, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how many of you were there on those two trucks?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was one of the escorts and there were two drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. And tell us, those armed soldiers who stopped you and told you you could not proceed, they were members of the HVO, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: They had HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what did they tell you? What army had put up barriers on the road and you could not move on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: In the next village, the next village was a Muslim village and they said that the BH army had put up barriers and one could not go through to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So how long did you stay in Sebesic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: We arrived in Sebesic around 8.00 in the morning on the 14th, spent the night there, and it was only around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. on the next day that small cars and buses were allowed to go through because there were many women and children so they let them move on to Vitez and onward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify this. Sebesic, the village of Sebesic is in what municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it should be Gornji Vakuf/Uskoplje and the next municipality is Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. And two days later you were then allowed to move on. So you spent the 14th there, the next day was the 15th. Was it then that they let you go that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 15th around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon. Only passenger cars and buses, no trucks. The trucks could not go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And tell us, this column of cars which was let through, how long was it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite long because vehicles had been coming up for the -- two days so it was quite big.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is for two days there was no traffic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, you arrived home sometime in the afternoon, or rather late afternoon you arrived, didn't you, on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived home around perhaps around 7.00 or perhaps 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And as you drove down the road, or when you arrived in your village, did you see anything unusual happening? Did you see perhaps any major concentration of troops, any major movements of troops or anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember well that it was a rainy day and it was already late afternoon, and on my way home, I did not notice anything out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you arrived home, you had a rest, went to bed, and what happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning, gunfire woke me up, so I got up. I was scared, surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And where did the sound of this gunfire come from?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, it seemed to me that I could hear it from all sides so I couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who was with you at home?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: My mother and I. My mother and I were alone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you go out of the house to see what was going on, who was firing and from where?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after I got up, some half hour later, perhaps, I went out. And at that moment my neighbour, a Muslim, came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is the name of that neighbour who came to see you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: That is Mr. Meho Kablar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, on what terms were you with Mr. Kablar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not really -- not only particular terms to write home about between me and him. But he was quite a good friend with my father because they were peers, more or less. I could be his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us what happened then, when Mr. Kablar came?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kablar came and he was visibly upset, just like myself; scared, just like I was. He asked me, "What was this," and I didn't know what it was. He suggested, since there are some five or six Croat houses next to my house, he suggested that all of us Croats should get into one house, women and children, everybody who was there, because we would be safer there. And that is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kablar is a Muslim, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So all of you who are Croats took shelter in one house because Mr. Kablar told you you would be safer there.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you what the danger was that you otherwise might be exposed to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I guessed -- I mean, he didn't say anything, but I guessed because there was gunfire from all sides and because perhaps that simply would be better if we all gathered in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything unusual happening around that house that you had moved into?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as we were moving into that house, and it took about half an hour or so until everybody got there. After that, we noticed that the house was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who surrounded the house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim soldiers had surrounded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many of you Croats were in the house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, men, women, and children, about 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you leave the house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we could not. But Mr. Kablar would come now and then, and he could go to our house, bring us some food. We dare not go out alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But if he escorted you, you could then go to your house and get some of your affairs.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Later on did Mr. Kablar come to that house in which you Croats were closed with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Later on in the afternoon, on the 16th, their commander arrived, the Muslim commander, and I was called to speak on behalf of the group which was imprisoned there. Their commander, speaking in front of Meho, he insisted that he should take men to prison, to Preocica, to Poculica, and that he would then let women and children go to Croat houses, that is, Buhine Kuce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who was that commander that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Osmancevic -- Osmancevic. I don't know his first name. I know his nickname; I remember we always called him Cike. But his first name just escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, did he live in the same village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were next-door neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So he wanted to take male Croats to prison and release women and children. How did Mr. Kablar react to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he reacted very vigorously. During all those talks and negotiations, he explained the situation to me from the time of World War II, that my father and his father had saved him and his family, so that he simply would not allow anyone to separate us from our families and to be imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You tell us that Mr. Kablar was an elderly man, that he was your father's peer. But what position was he in the village? Was he a well-respected figure there; could you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was -- yes, he did enjoy prestige in the village as far as the Muslim part of the population was concerned, because he was an honest man, of integrity, a man who kept his word, and what he said was respected by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. So what happened next?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened is that on the 17th, around perhaps 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon, Mr. Kablar escorted us from the village and took us to Croat houses, so that at long last we joined our own folk, that is, Croat houses. And that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Miskovic, while you were in that house in the village - that was the 16th and the major part of the 17th of April - was there any gunfire in the village? Were there any combat operations that you might have heard or seen?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we could not really see much from the house, and we could hear the gunfire. Now, where it came from, at that time we really could not know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. So Mr. Kablar escorted all of you who were in that house to the territory controlled by the HVO units, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we came down -- as I said, in the beginning the village was mixed, and next to the main road, the majority of the houses were Croat. So that when we got down there, there was no police or anybody. There were only the local residents, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So next to the main road at that time there were no combat operations or anything.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, there was nothing. There were just the local residents in their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened to your house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: My house perished. All my property, everything, was burnt down so that to this day, I mean, it's like that. Nothing's been rebuilt yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that day, the 17th of April, did you ever manage to get back to your house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did. The first time, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you cannot live in it to this day.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, because everything's been burnt down. All the property there has been burnt so that I cannot live there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about your belongings that you had in the house and in the farm buildings?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really tell you because I didn't -- I never managed to get anything out of the house. And what was burnt down, what was looted, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. And what happened then? After you reached the first Croat houses, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: In that part, those Croat houses where we -- when we got there, there were some 15 men, and we all got together and we realised that we had to set up some front line against Muslim forces. And that evening, that is on the 15th of April, those 15 neighbours elected me as a would-be commander or something like that. We organised ourselves, since we were 15 of us, then four of us should take positions next to houses so as to form a kind of a line against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of armament did you have with those local residents there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the weapons were not much, really, a couple of rifles, a couple of hunting rifles, perhaps a couple of automatic rifles. Nothing much, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any trenches prepared in advance that you could take?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I mean we were all -- no, it was just an extraordinary situation. We were all frightened and scared and confused. We didn't know where to make a trench or how to make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And after a while, did anyone come to give you some instructions as to what and how to do it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of days later, Mr. Bertovic arrived. He said that he was a major, that he came to us on behalf of the Vitez Brigade, and then he told us how to organise ourselves, how to position ourselves and ordered us to dig trenches. We had already begun to do that, but I'm afraid we were not particularly successful at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. But let us now try to place this Mr. Bertovic in your village in some time context. If you were released on the 17th of April and then you went down to the lower part of the village, so after how many days did Bertovic come to see you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some three or four days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it would be sometime after the 20th of April, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really tell you exactly now but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you tell us that Mr. Bertovic introduced himself to you as a major of the Vitez Brigade, that he explained to you where to dig trenches. Did he then tell you anything about your status, I mean your military status?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember him saying anything. I know we simply began to feel better because somebody had come who was to look after things. We were just simple civilians. We knew nothing, and at least there was somebody who could issue orders. There was some kind of a chain of command which we had to obey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But did you realise at some point that you had become members of the Vitez Brigade since Bertovic, who introduced himself to you as a major of the Vitez Brigade, in a manner of speaking, issued orders to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well you could say that when he came there and organised us, yes, you could say that by the very -- by this very fact, yes, we became members of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you get any military IDs or any written document about your affiliation, about your membership in the Vitez Brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, we were not given anything. Whether Mr. Bertovic had kept any record or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that your neighbours elected you their commander, but what happened after that and how long did you stay at that line in the village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Very, very short time, because in -- when I served in the JNA, I was with the engineering unit so they called me to join the engineering unit of the Vitez Brigade, and I was happy to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And who was your commander there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Ivica Drmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was your chief role in the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the engineer -- the engineering troops had to protect that line which had been established, fortified to try to proper -- to secure those lines, to devise some devices to fortify them and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that at the time when you served the former JNA, you had acquired some professional knowledge in engineering. How would you describe your activity and the activity of the engineering unit of the Vitez Brigade in those days? Would you say that it was engaged in some defensive, offensive or perhaps some third role?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in those days, we simply were trying to stop the advancement of Muslim forces, that is, to protect as much as possible the front line that had already been established with all the devices, with all the resources available to the engineering unit at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how long were you with the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where do you live today, Mr. Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I live in Vitez today as -- in a rented apartment because I have not settled my question of accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that your house was burned down. Have you done anything to reconstruct it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I was promised by the municipal authorities, and especially the department for reconstruction and development, that they would help me in reconstructing my house, but so far, nothing has come of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: According to what you have just told us, you became a member of those military units of the Vitez Brigade after the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see any official documents on your participation -- concerning your participation in the resistance, the armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: All that I can tell you about that was that I asked to get some of the certificates that they were giving out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And were you given the right to put your name down for receiving those certificates?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what did you do with the certificates you obtained?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing so far. I'm waiting for the reconstruction of the factory that I am working in, for it to be reorganised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Miskovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of Mr. Kordic has no questions to ask this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, in 1992, did you know a man called Buha who lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give me a date, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: October 1992, a local HVO commander called Buha, B-u-h-a, I think.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that man as a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard that in October 1992, he gave an ultimatum to local Muslims to hand in their weapons. Did you hear anything of his doing that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember now. At that time I was not in the village, so I cannot tell you whether that particular gentleman issued such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1992, did you still have a function as a reservist, especially in light of your military training? Did you have a function as a reservist?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, 1991, I was put on standby and I engaged in some private business together with my brother so that I did not become a part of any reserve formation. As far as the army is concerned, I did not contact anybody. I had nothing to do with the army. I worked privately and was engaged in private business.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you understand yourself to be under a general duty to be mobilised when anybody wanted you to be -- or not when anybody, when the HVO wanted you to be?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I was sufficiently well-acquainted with everything via the media, television and so on, but I never thought that anybody could mobilise me, and I didn't think that any conflicts would take place in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, for 1992, the refugees coming down to your part of the valley were by no means all Muslim or anything like it, the majority of them were probably Croats to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the refugees go in my area, I know from my own village, that the Muslim refugees remained there, but as far as the rest of the municipality goes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your village, I think, had a majority of Croat houses, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: In my village, the make-up of the population was 50/50, half, half.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm just putting to you evidence that we've had from elsewhere, but in the wider population, yes, 50/50, but in Buhine Kuce, was that mostly Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Up by the main road they were mostly Muslims, but as my own house is 300 metres away from the main road, that means the Croats were a minority in that region as far as the Muslims are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have spoken of some digging of trenches you say by Muslims in the period before the outbreak of fighting, but there was no preparation for fighting by either side in the period before the 16th of April, was there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the preparations were, but there was an ugly feeling. These Muslim trenches were dug in front of our houses, and the trenches that were dug around Mr. Dzidic's house, who was a member of the municipal Crisis Staff at that time, or a post to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well this all followed months and months of the HVO taking over Vitez, didn't it, or don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the taking over of power, the Muslims and Croats took over power and authority in Vitez after the first free elections so that a municipal council was set up according to the principle of the number of votes that everybody got. And the Crisis Staff was set up on that basis so there's no need to speak of any takeover of control because it didn't actually take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your private business, was that to do with humanitarian aid or was that something else?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't have anything to do with humanitarian aid. My brother has a veterinary pharmacy, an agricultural pharmacy, and that's the line of business we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the morning of the 16th of April, you really tell us you don't know where the firing came from?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I was woken up by the shooting. I got up. But where it was coming from, I don't know. It seemed to me that it was coming from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first realise that Santici and Ahmici, which is a kilometre or so at most from your house, when did you first realise they were being attacked by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: For two days we were shut up in a Croatian house, and what was going on in Ahmici and Santici, we heard about that only at the end of the day of the 17th. We heard that it was the defence of Croatian villages, that's what we heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Well who told you this then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: We received that information from the people down there when we got down there among the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the Croats said they'd simply been defending themselves, did they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. And you accepted that at the time, and you accept it still, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first information that I heard. It was only later on in time that I heard what had happened, especially in Ahmici, and this took on a different dimension.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you hear had happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that a terrible crime had taken place, which I myself, as an individual, just like everyone else, any normal person, condemned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who'd done it? Who committed this crime?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have only a couple more questions for you. Thank you. You stayed in this house for a couple of days, and you say that you were, as it were, mobilised into the Viteska Brigade by Anto Bertovic; have I understood it correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No; that is to say, for two days I was detained. We were in an encirclement, in a house, those of us Croats who had remained there. It was only in the afternoon of the 17th, at about 6.00 p.m., when we were escorted by Mr. Kablar to the Hrvatska Kuce, and that's where I met my Croat neighbours who were in their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the formality of being made a member of the Viteska Brigade? What did he say had happened so that you suddenly became a member of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: In my testimony I emphasised that we were there alone for a few days. We were ordinary civilians, and we tried to do what we could to set up a front line towards the Muslim side. With Mr. Bertovic's arrival several days later, while we were down there, he would give us instructions how to organise the defence line towards the Muslims, and he said that they had just come from the Vitez Brigade to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His commander was Cerkez, wasn't it, Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just quickly look at this document, just to give completeness, 1461.4. This document suggests that you were made a -- sorry, I should explain the document to you in case you haven't seen it or haven't seen it recently. The 1st of November, 1994, this document, appears to be signed by Mario Cerkez, and it confirms that you, born in 1964, have been a member of the HVO Vitez Brigade since the 16th of April of 1993, and that you were wounded in the SPS Vitez on the 5th of November, 1993. As to that date, the 16th of April, 1993, can you explain why it's there, if he really only came and told you days later you were mobilised after you had been imprisoned or detained?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the confirmation was issued on the 1st of November, 1994. As a wounded person, I went before a commission to determine my invalidity, the degree to which I had been injured. We see that it is the Croatian Defence Council, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was issued to me by the regiment for this medical board --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But why the 16th of April? That's all. Or is the truth that you were, as it were, signed up a little earlier than the 19th and that you were active as early as the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't have been in the brigade on duty before, because on the 16th I was taken prisoner, on the 16th/17th. And this is just a bureaucratic piece of paper. These are facts and figures --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. The other reason I ask you that is this: We've heard from a witness, at page 23630, Dragan Cickovic, that between the 16th and 18th of April, this part of the area, your village, was changing hands all the time; first one side held it and then another did. Does that fit with your recollection of events?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: From the 16th to the 18th, that is to say, from the -- I can speak about the 17th onwards. Because the Croatian houses in that village are bordering on Sivrino Selo, so to the north you have Sivrino Selo.
