And from the 17th, when I went down there with my neighbours, there was no movement of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. The last thing, I want you to look at a page - I've got the document and I'll make it available for the ELMO - it's part of 652.3 [sic], and it's a list of people assigned to the line on the HVO side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. It better go in then. Sorry. Thank you very much. My mistake. It's a new document. I only want the witness to look at it for one purpose. Document 852.3. The transcript is wrong. If the usher would be good enough to show the witness the list of names, and it's where the numbers start at 72 and go onwards to 149.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this list of names, please, it's a list of names of people deployed, and your name appears at number 100, I think. What I want your help with for the moment is this: If we look at number 100, "Miskovic Josip," we can see that the names surrounding it are not in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. alphabetical order. They go "Vidovic Zoran, Papic Anto," then your name, then "Djotlo Nikola, Bevanda Franjo," and so on. Now, in case it becomes relevant, can you tell us, are the names surrounding your name names with your village, or are they just simply, as it were, names at random reflecting they're also being joined up to the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you that Josip -- there are three or four Josip Miskovics in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: So I couldn't say that that is actually me, my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Well, do the names surrounding your name come from your village, then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not sure that the Josip Miskovic here is me; secondly, of these names here, I think that as far as I am able to recognise certain individuals, I don't think it is one village, I think that they are people from different villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, Your Honour, probably this witness can't help us with this document, and I'll get somebody else later who can. That's all I have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miskovic, I have one more question for you. You were asked by the Prosecutor about the movement of lines in your village. When were the lines in your village moved, shifted? At the middle of 1993, in the period when you were there, or did that take place later on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I stress that on the 16th and 17th I had been taken prisoner. From the 17th, in the evening onwards, until -- and I was in Buhine Kuce, there was no shifting. But the shifting took place at the end of 1993 and the beginning of 1994, when the Muslim forces attacked Buhine Kuce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that answer. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Taraba. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal. For the record, could you give us your full name and place and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: My name is Vlado Taraba and I was born on the 14th of October, 1959 in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I am also going to ask you, Mr. Taraba, just as you have been doing, to speak slowly and leave a pause between my question and your answer and of course vice versa, I shall wait for you to finish what you are saying to facilitate the interpreters' job. You are by nationality a Croat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you are Roman Catholic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you have dual citizenship?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you are a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do the laws of those countries allow you to have dual citizenship?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are, by profession -- could you tell us what you are?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: By profession, I am a teacher of protection and national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What does that subject imply? You graduated from university in the former Yugoslavia. Now what does this entail, this faculty for national defence and protection? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: It was part of the political science faculty in Sarajevo and it was aimed at training students to become teachers of protection and national defence and to be able to teach in schools. And this was a specific subject taught in the former Yugoslavia, and it also capacitated pupils to work in the internal affairs department and in security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did this include work in Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Taraba, as you're here and you have that professional training and expertise, let me ask you one further question by way of introduction: Is it true that the former Yugoslavia developed and had a system of what was called "total national defence" or "all peoples' national defence"?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What did that mean? What did that system mean for the defence of the country in case of war?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: The system of total national defence and social self-protection, as it was called in the former Yugoslavia, was aimed at training a broad section of the population in matters of defence, to be able to defend the country should there be a foreign aggressor, whether from neighbouring countries, the NATO pact or the Warsaw pact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this concept of total national defence and social self-protection included, in part, the fact that each citizen, each and every citizen, unless he had already been given an assignment, should a mobilisation arise to join the reserves of the JNA or reserve forces of any kind or have work assignments, that he would stay in his home and in his village to protect them. Was that the premise?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Or similarly, that workers in a socially-owned enterprise should protect that enterprise?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, that was regulated by the laws and regulations of the former state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Taraba, today you are an officer of the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes. I am a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before the beginning of the war, I mean the war before 1992, you worked as a professor in a school; is that right, you taught? What school was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: That was the secondary school centre of Boris Kidric located in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When did you cease performing that function?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: I stopped being a teacher in the school at the beginning of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time, did your involvement begin in the 2nd Brigade of Stjepan Tomasevic, 2nd Battalion of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And as a member of the command of the 2nd Battalion, what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: I was in charge -- I was a deputy commander for education and training and operational affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you explain in a word what this meant? What was your job? What did you actually do at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Well, my job was mainly to keep records of groups going to the defence lines against the army of Republika Srpska or rather at that time it was the former JNA, and I kept records of who went to the front line and what weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: I apologise, may I add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Among other things, I was charged with overseeing the change of shifts on the defence line in the Strikanica and Slatka Voda line against the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, we'll come to that later. In early December 1992 when you joined the command of the 2nd Battalion of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, was it already functioning or was it just being established? Were you in the first group of people in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, in early December was when the brigade was formed, so I was among the first people to become members of the brigade after it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when did you leave the brigade? When did you stop being part of this brigade, Stjepan Tomasevic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: We stopped being part of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade when the Viteska Brigade was formed, and as far as I can remember, that was the end of February or the beginning of March. That's when I think the Vitez Brigade was formed.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And your battalion was then re-organised and changed its name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes. It was no longer the 2nd Battalion of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, it was now the 1st Battalion of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And a new command was established, mostly new; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Do you mean the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now stick to 1992 for a while so as to have the events in the correct order. You already mentioned that you kept records of men and weapons. Did you have or did you perform any activities in connection with organising village patrols?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: With respect to the organisation of village patrols, I had an advisory role because they were mostly elderly men or men who were not able bodied for military service. And they saw me, let's say, as an expert in this area so they turned to me for advice and for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Taraba, this advisory role was this something that you undertook at someone's orders?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it on your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, at the initiative of my fellow villagers in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What villages are we talking about? Where did you give advice in this way to help in the organisation of village patrols?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: First of all, I am referring to my hamlet, Marosove Kuce and then Stara Bila which are in a narrow area, and it was easy to have contacts with people and give them advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were they villages in the immediate vicinity of your -- the place where you lived?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you, as a citizen, an inhabitant of one of those villages, did you feel duty-bound, in a moral sense, to help in the organisation of village patrols?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, of course I felt it was my moral duty because it was obvious that there was a war raging in Croatia, that the units of the former JNA were already in the areas nearby and there were local bandits, so to speak, who made use of these circumstances for their own benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And who organised the village patrols?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: The village patrols were mostly self-organised, the people from the village. For example, some elderly people who had a good reputation whom other people looked up to, who had authority among their neighbours, and they organised it. So it was organised by people themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, their reason, their motive for this was the presence of the JNA in the area and also the increase in crime, various gangs of criminals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you were part of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, in your battalion, and later on in the Vitez Brigade, did you ever receive the task, or in general, was it your duty to organise village patrols?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In 1992, while you were in your village, did the village patrols at least in your village and the villages nearby, function? Did they function properly? Can you describe this very briefly?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Well, the patrols functioned relatively well because people saw the need to protect themselves in a way. There were also people who refused to go and made excuses that they had other duties but, in general, they did function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what did they, in fact, do, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we've had a very considerable amount of detail about this and the village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, then I will not continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Taraba, do you remember later on in 1993 or late 1992 and 1993, were there people from your village who went to take shifts in the direction of Vlasic, Turbe, Jajce, in other places where the HVO were active, as active soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you give an estimate how many such men were there in your village of Marosi in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: I couldn't say the number of men exactly, but it's a relatively small village and a lot of young people were working abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did the Stjepan Tomasevic, or rather your battalion whether it was part of Stjepan Tomasevic or later from March onwards part of the Vitez Brigade, did it hold lines, the line from Strikanci to Slatka Vode?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was the line facing the JNA and the army of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned that -- we don't want to weary the Trial Chamber, but could you describe your role as regards these shifts?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: My role was simply to take the men from various villages, to be with them, to go to Strikanica to Slatka Vode with them, and then there would be a change of shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you had to inform a certain number of men that on such and such a date they would be going to perform such and such a task?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: A few days before, as a rule. We told the coordinators in the villages that they were to prepare a shift, a certain number of men, that is, to go to the defence line against the army of Republika Srpska in the sector you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was a certain time and place from which that group would go to the location you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And according to plan, how large was the group supposed to be for you to man your sector?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, between 50 and 60 men in a group. But we rarely had the right number of men. There was always someone who was sick, someone who couldn't come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If someone did not wish to respond and they said they were ill or went on a journey to avoid going, could they have done that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: There were such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we say that your soldiers responded, in fact, on a voluntary basis?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Well, they had a moral obligation. It was voluntary, but if they did not respond, they would be morally condemned by their neighbours who did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you would gather them together in a certain place, at a certain time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have a great deal of evidence about this too. The witness has described what he did in terms of organisation, and all this detail doesn't really help us. In fact, it confuses things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point was -- of course, I will not enter it further. But the idea was just that we have a person who was constantly monitoring that project.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there's any dispute about it, he can be cross-examined and if necessary you can re-examine him. Can we move on now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to show the witness Z653. [In English] Would you put the English on the ELMO and the original to the witness. I'm apologising for not announcing that document in front, but I think that I put it -- yes, I did put it in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Taraba, first I will ask you, have you ever seen this document before or, rather, did you see it then, during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will draw your attention to the place where there should be a signature but there is only a post. Can you explain what it means?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: That was the person who dealt with security in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, do you believe that your battalion produced this document? And this follows from the signature and from the heading.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Judging by the heading and the signature, I believe it did. Although there is no actual signature of a person, but this type -- that's what the documents looked like in general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps on the 14th of April, when this document was drawn up, who was performing this function in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Whether it was Mr. Zarko Saric, I don't know, but I think it was -- I think it was either him or the late Mr. Ivan Budimir. I cannot be absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me the following, please: First of all, what does SIS mean? That is an acronym in the heading and in the signature.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: As far as I know, it means Security Information Service. Yes, Security Information Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that it was an intelligence service within your battalion?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: I think there was a person who was in charge of military intelligence, and that was VOS. Those would be the letters used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the basis of what were jobs assigned? What was the duty of SIS and what was the duty of VOS, if you can explain that very briefly?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: I think that the task of SIS was to deal with security inside the unit; the task of VOS was to gather information about the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does it mean any other enemy too, I mean, regardless of who that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let's go back to SIS. In view of the education that you received and what you have just told us, would it be the task of SIS to establish the possible source of recruits, soldiers, that could be counted upon if need be?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: This could be obtained from the defence office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did the records of the defence office reflect the real situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: By and large, yes. Even though it did happen that, for instance, my late uncle, who died in 1977, was also on the files there, and it was in late 1993 -- yes, late 1993, they issued a summons to him, they wanted to call him up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Finally, look at this document. Under 2, your village and neighbouring villages are mentioned here - perhaps you are more or less familiar with them - and also the number of soldiers is indicated. Could you tell me if the number of soldiers indicated next to the name of the villages tally with the number of those that you used to form your unit? If you do not know exactly, then tell us approximately, or no. I don't know if you know it at all, or do you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Well, it's roughly there. Perhaps a little more, perhaps a little less, but roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Above that group of villages, it says: "Second Company - Commander, Slavko Badrov." Tell us, please, at that time in those villages, was there a company formed, or does this mean a company that should be formed before you undertake an operation?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: At that time companies existed on paper only, which means that these are men who should become some of those men who went to take shifts against the army of Republika Srpska, to just have some kind of a record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My last question about this: Would you agree that this overview is the estimate that was done by the battalion regarding the possibilities of defence in your villages, possible strength of troops in your villages?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Taraba, in the early days of the Vitez Brigade, you have already told us it only had one battalion, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you identify the time when, as the conflict escalated, as of the 16th of April, 1993, other battalions formed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out, it could have been six or seven days later that the defence areas were formed, and areas comprised individual villages. So I should think it was in July, end of July, but I'm not quite sure of that, defence sectors grew into battalions of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, how many battalions were there in early 1994, that is, just before the war ended?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In March 1993, where was the seat of your battalion's command?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: The headquarters of my battalion was in the administrative building of Sumarija, at Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where it was before that, while you were still a part of Stjepan Tomasevic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: It was in the building which housed the cinema.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember why you moved from the cinema building to Sumarija?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: I think it was because the brigade headquarters was now in this cinema.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, the command of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So as not to go back to this, or perhaps we shouldn't open an area for cross-examination which is not necessary. So the command post of the battalion then moved to a third address. Do you know where that was?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA
utterances.text: I think that it was the building -- rather, a building within the Impregnacija compound, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I won't ask any further questions about that location. We have heard enough. Your Honour, if I may ask, are you planning for a longer day, or we will finish as regular so I can plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Regular hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We want to hear a bit about your plans, so it may be just as well if we conclude the witness now and go on in the morning. How much longer do you anticipate being with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Surely not more than half an hour. There is one issue. If I may point out, paragraph 4.2, I am unfortunately waiting for the translation from the Registry; I was promised to get it today but so far I haven't. Because I think that is a unique opportunity to use the witness who said he would be able to recognise the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Taraba, we are adjourning now as far as you are concerned. Could you come back, please, tomorrow morning at half past nine to conclude your evidence? Would you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include members of the Defence team. Thank you very much. If you'd like to go now and be back at half past nine tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, any question to a witness beginning "Do you agree with" is likely to be leading. Could you bear that in mind? There was one just now on rather an important issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There was. I apologise, Your Honour. There was no objection in advance to the summary, so I was simply looking for the further -- for a faster advance. But I will not do it, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the state of play now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may ask the usher -- unfortunately, the usher is now out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ask the Registrar to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have put this in telegraphic form. Since we are talking about the numbers and the days, probably it would be better if you could distribute it to everybody. As you can see, Your Honours, we analysed the situation up to Saturday late afternoon when we prepared this paper. Even though there are some little differences in numbers, and even though that in the meantime, this example only of how precise I would forecast may be, but in the meantime I got information that my expert witness is on the operation in the hospital. So you never know how the things are changing because we are dealing with a relatively big number of persons coming from different areas with many other specific problems. Nevertheless, first of all, we think that last couple of days clearly showed good progress and we think that, based on that progress including today, that that entitled us to plan the rest of the case rather optimistically. We would like to see about 40 witnesses in the courtroom until the end of the case but unfortunately, I don't think that we will have more than optimistically 36, 37 if we are lucky. We also did make a plan for weeks in details, we know who is coming when. It is about ten witnesses to be called during the week of 25 September, then three witnesses during the short week of October 2, and then about 11, 12, originally planned 13, will be called on the week of 9 October. There is contingency. If all the planned witnesses for the week of 9 October would appear, probably one or two would be prolonged on Monday for the week of I guess that is 16 October, the last week of our Defence, anyway. Then during that last week, we would like to have the testimony of our client. We will try to prepare that efficiently so that it will not take, for direct examination, more than two days. We are not planning something like was seen in Blaskic case going in minutes by minutes, hour and hour. Simply, if for nothing else, than for practical reasons our client does not have such records to follow which Mr. Blaskic did. If we can agree that, roughly speaking, there shall be at least general balance of time spent, then we obviously could count on four days maximum, so up to two days for the direct and up to two days for cross-examination. I would just like to conclude that we believe that that is feasible. It is perhaps a little bit tight, but with all due respect, we hope that we really can deliver that providing that some additional time will not be taken from us like from, for example, I don't have an idea when those two witnesses which are subpoenaed will arrive and if they will, I would kindly ask that this time would not be taken from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It can't be taken from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And only maybe to explain there is also mentioning of one -- I use the term "standard witness" in the -- I guess you understand, but also substantial witness and this witness is already given on batting order to my dear colleagues, it is Captain Anto Bertovic. We cannot put him on short direct examination like other witnesses, because there are surely several subjects; he has to explain what was going on from his perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When are you minded to call him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We are planning to have him in this short week as the first witness or perhaps if one or two, but extremely short witnesses from the previous week will not be finished on the Friday of the previous week, when perhaps we will finish first those two, but we are planning in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a way that last witnesses from previous -- or a week which preceded the short week, that those last witnesses are really short, just a small picture in and out and we can do it in -- altogether with cross and direct in less than an hour, I guess. Anyway, then Mr. Bertovic would be able to start on first trial day in that short week and then we have two short witnesses just in order to fill in all the time which may remain. Your Honour, we really did the best we can. We consider it also additional affidavits, we did find two, but unfortunately, we are not able to relocate some witnesses originally planned for live testimony to the category of affidavits simply because we have no vehicle to attach him to something. But we are planning quite a big number of affidavits which are connected to so-called Spork binders where there is obviously no sense to get another, I don't know, 50 people to have their testimony on how and why they were recorded in those listings. So we will have an officer who was involved in that process during the war and after the war who, either directly or indirectly, was involved in production of those various listings, at least some of them, and who knows about technology, and it is through that witness based on the examples the witness will use, we can use the affidavits. I wouldn't have anything more to add. If you have any questions, I will be delighted to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Well, thank you very much, Mr. Kovacic. We appreciate your efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that timetable is followed, then clearly that would be satisfactory as far as the timing of the case is concerned. Let me say this about the timing of the case, that we intend to stick to the timetable but, as you may have heard, the case which we were going to hear in November has had to go off and, as a result, there will be two weeks in reserve. Now, that is not to encourage anybody to think of calling more evidence, the words are "in reserve". It may be that it will be necessary to call the Court witnesses during that period which we'll have to consider, but that apart, we do not anticipate calling any or having any other evidence during the period, but they are in reserve which brings me to something I ought to deal with in closed session. Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 4.16 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday the 19th day of September, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
